title: The case for 1 John 5:7
subtitle: "There are three that bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit, and these three are one."
summary: A textual and patristic defense of the Comma Johanneum: its presence in the Vetus Latina, Cyprian's witness, the Codex Fuldensis preface, the 484 Council of Carthage, and the chain of Latin Fathers who quote it as Scripture before the Vulgate.
origin: Discord, dogma-exegesis: The Case for 1 John 5:7.

essay.text: 1 John 5:7, the Comma Johanneum, remains a focal point of textual and theological debate. Critics, including many academics and antitrinitarian polemicists, challenge the verse on the grounds of its absence from the earliest extant Greek manuscripts and conclude that it is a later interpolation. A serious counter-case persists, rooted in the Latin manuscript tradition. The Comma appears in Latin witnesses by the fourth century and is treated as Scripture in earlier patristic citation, suggesting it was integrated into Western Christian texts well before the formalisation of the Vulgate.

Cyprian of Carthage (mid-third century) writes in On the Unity of the Church: "The Lord says, I and the Father are one; and again it is written of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, And these three are one." Cyprian wrote in Latin from a pre-Vulgate Old Latin (Vetus Latina) text. Latin translations of the New Testament are based on Greek manuscripts circulating in the early Church; if the phrase "these three are one" stood in Cyprian's Old Latin, it traces back through a Greek exemplar that pre-dated him.

Cyprian does not quote the entire Comma. He uses the shorthand "these three are one" (et tres unum sunt), which he expressly presents as "written" (scriptum est) of the Trinity. Allegorical readings of the eighth verse (water, blood, spirit) cannot account for this, he argues from express Scripture of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, the language of v. 7.

The Codex Fuldensis, copied in 546, contains a preface to the Canonical Epistles that explicitly defends the Comma against unfaithful copyists who had dropped the testimony of the Father, the Word, and the Spirit. The preface says: "Where we read about the unity of the Trinity in the First Epistle of John, we have discovered that much error has arisen from unfaithful translators, who, disregarding the truth of the faith, included only the three terms, water, blood, and spirit, in their version, while omitting the testimony of the Father, the Word, and the Spirit." This is a sixth-century witness from the Vulgate tradition itself that the verse was being deliberately removed by some hands, not added by others.

In 484, at the command of the Arian Vandal king Huneric, a council was convened in Carthage. The king sought to coerce the orthodox episcopate; 461 bishops from Africa, Mauritania, Sardinia, Corsica, and the Balearic Isles stood in defence of the Godhead. They were led by Eugenius of Carthage. Central to their defence was 1 John 5:7. Eugenius' manifesto, the Liber Fidei Catholicae, invokes the Comma directly: "And so, to teach even more clearly that the Holy Spirit is of the same divine essence with the Father and the Son, the testimony of John the Evangelist confirms this. For he says: There are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit, and these three are one."

Fulgentius of Ruspe, in the early sixth century, cites the Comma as Apostle John's own testimony, and footnotes Cyprian as having confirmed it. Cassiodorus echoes the Comma in his Complexiones on the apostolic Epistles. Phoebadius, in the fourth century, quotes a recognisably equivalent confession in the West. The chain is unbroken from the third century to the sixth, on Latin patristic grounds, before any later medieval editorial activity could plausibly have inserted the verse.

florilegium.author: St Cyprian of Carthage
florilegium.work: On the Unity of the Church
florilegium.text: The Lord says, "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30); and again it is written of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, "And these three are one." And does anyone believe that this unity, which thus comes from the divine strength and coheres in celestial sacraments, can be divided in the Church, and can be separated by the parting asunder of opposing wills?
florilegium.gloss: The earliest patristic citation. Cyprian quotes 1 John 5:7 as Scripture and pairs it with John 10:30 to ground the unity of the Trinity, c. 250.

florilegium.author: St Cyprian of Carthage
florilegium.work: Letter 72, to Jubaianus, On the Baptism of Heretics
florilegium.text: If of the Holy Spirit, since the three are one, how can the Holy Spirit be at peace with him who is the enemy either of the Son or of the Father?
florilegium.gloss: Cyprian again, in a different work, invokes the formula "the three are one" as a given of Christian Scripture, in a discussion of baptism and the Holy Spirit.

florilegium.author: Codex Fuldensis, Preface to the Canonical Epistles
florilegium.text: Where we read about the unity of the Trinity in the First Epistle of John, we have discovered that much error has arisen from unfaithful translators, who, disregarding the truth of the faith, included only the three terms, water, blood, and spirit, in their version, while omitting the testimony of the Father, the Word, and the Spirit.
florilegium.original: ubi de unitate trinitatis in prima iohannis epistula positum legimus in qua est ab infidelibus translatoribus multum erratum esse fidei ueritate conperimus trium tantummodo uocabula hoc est aquae sanguinis et spiritus in ipsa sua editione potentes et patri uerbique ac spiritus testimonium omittentes.
florilegium.gloss: A sixth-century witness from within the Vulgate tradition that the Comma was being suppressed by some translators, not invented by later ones.

florilegium.author: The Council of Carthage (Eugenius of Carthage)
florilegium.reference: as preserved by Victor of Vita (PL 58)
florilegium.text: And so, to teach even more clearly that the Holy Spirit is of the same divine essence with the Father and the Son, the testimony of John the Evangelist confirms this. For he says: "There are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit, and these three are one."
florilegium.original: Et ut adhuc luce clarius unius divinitatis esse cum Patre et Filio Spiritum sanctum doceamus, Joannis evangelistae testimonio comprobatur. Ait namque: "Tres sunt qui testimonium perhibent in caelo: Pater, Verbum, et Spiritus sanctus, et hi tres unum sunt."
florilegium.gloss: 461 orthodox bishops of North Africa, before an Arian king, cite the Comma as conciliar Scripture. The verse is not a private medieval insertion.

florilegium.author: St Fulgentius of Ruspe
florilegium.text: In the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, we acknowledge the unity of substance, but we do not confuse the persons. For the blessed John the Apostle testifies, saying: "There are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Spirit; and these three are one" (1 John 5:7). The most blessed martyr Cyprian also confirms this in his letter on the Unity of the Church.
florilegium.gloss: Fulgentius, early sixth century, quotes the Comma by name as the Apostle John's testimony, and footnotes Cyprian as having quoted it before him.

florilegium.author: Cassiodorus
florilegium.text: And the three mysteries testify on earth: water, blood, and spirit, the fulfilment of which we read about in the Passion of the Lord. And in heaven: Father and Son and Holy Spirit. And these three are one God.
florilegium.original: Cui rei testificantur in terra tria mysteria: aqua, sanguis et spiritus, quae in passione Domini leguntur impleta: in coelo autem Pater, et Filius, et Spiritus sanctus, et hi tres unus est Deus.
florilegium.gloss: Cassiodorus expressly distinguishes the earthly witnesses (v. 8) from the heavenly witnesses (v. 7), and ascribes both to the same passage.

florilegium.author: Tertullian (as adduced by James Bennett)
florilegium.work: Against Praxeas (cf. Bennett, Theology of the Early Christian Church, p. 94)
florilegium.reference: cf. Adversus Praxean, on "these three are one thing"
florilegium.text: Thus the connection of the Father in the Son, and of the Son in the Paraclete, produces three coherent Persons, who are yet distinct one from another. These three are one essence.
florilegium.gloss: Bennett shows Tertullian quoting the disputed formula in the same idiom (unum, not unus), substance, not person, which is how Cyprian and the later Latins read 1 John 5:7.

florilegium.author: Pseudo-Athanasius
florilegium.text: And what about that sin-remitting, life-giving, and sanctifying washing (baptism), without which no one will see the kingdom of heaven, which is given to the faithful in the Thrice-Blessed Name? In addition to all these, John says, "And these three are one."
florilegium.original: Τί δὲ καὶ τὸ τῆς ἀφέσεως τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν παρεκτικὸν, καὶ ζωοποιὸν, καὶ ἁγιαστικὸν λουτρὸν, οὗ χωρὶς οὐδεὶς ὄψεται τὴν βασιλείαν τῶν οὐρανῶν, οὐκ ἐν τῇ τρισμακαρίᾳ ὀνομασίᾳ δίδοται τοῖς πιστοῖς; Πρὸς τούτοις πᾶσιν Ἰωάννης φάσκει· «Καὶ οἱ τρεῖς τὸ ἕν εἰσιν».
florilegium.gloss: A Greek witness, even outside the Latin tradition, that the apostle John's formula "the three are one" was being read in baptismal Trinitarian context.

councils.name: Council of Carthage (against the Arians)
councils.reference: Liber Fidei Catholicae (per Victor of Vita)
councils.text: There are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit, and these three are one.
councils.gloss: 461 orthodox bishops of North Africa, in confession against the Arian Vandals, cite 1 John 5:7 as Scripture. The Comma is a conciliar text, not a private gloss.

scripture.note: The Comma itself, in its Trinitarian form.
The earthly witnesses, water, blood, spirit, which the Fathers distinguish from the heavenly witnesses of v. 7.
Cyprian pairs this directly with 1 John 5:7.
The baptismal Trinitarian name, often paired with the Comma in patristic argument.
